The far more valuable thing here is the PIPELINE, which should be copied into the Element Picker's capture step regardless of whether we install the package: clone the node, compute and copy the resolved style for the node and every descendant onto the clone including pseudo-elements, find all @font-face declarations and download and base64-inline the font files, inline img sources and CSS background images, then serialise. Steps three and four are what make a capture genuinely OFFLINE-COMPLETE rather than a set of dangling URLs, and offline completeness is a hard constraint for us.

Second and more decisive architecturally: UIED solves the problem of recovering UI elements from a SCREENSHOT using computer vision, and we do not have that problem — the Element Picker hands us the real DOM with resolved CSS, which is ground truth. best_three: Fix the token format before writing any colour code: adopt DTCG .tokens.json (version 2025.10, verified Stable as of 2025-10-28) as the on-disk format for the colour system and template presets, then make the palette self-populating by running @projectwallace/css-analyzer (MIT, published 2026-07-27) over CSS captured by the Element Picker — it returns the distinct colours, font-sizes, spacing values, shadows and radii a real site actually uses. This turns the owner's 'build a colour system' request into a one-click extraction instead of manual work, and because DTCG is a published standard it simultaneously delivers all three hand-off routes for free: the ZIP gets a schema-described token file, the Markdown route gets trivially readable JSON, and Penpot/Figma/Tokens Studio/Style Dictionary interop costs us zero code. Do this first because it is the cheapest decision here and every later feature persists through it.

Build the Element-Picker ingest pipeline on three drop-in, permissive, framework-free libraries that together make a capture SEMANTIC rather than a blob: css-tree (MIT, v3.2.1) to parse, walk, prune and regenerate the hundreds of junk declarations in resolved CSS; html-aria (MIT, ARIA 1.3, zero dependencies, 40 stars) to answer what each captured node actually IS by resolving its real ARIA role from tag plus attributes plus ancestors; and dom-accessibility-api (MIT, the accname implementation behind Testing Library) to answer what it is CALLED. The output is a layers panel reading 'Submit button, Search field, Product card' instead of 'div, div, path' — which is precisely the gap between the owner's current loose shapes and the mature UI design he asked for, and all three run from vanilla TS with no framework and no network.

Implement component-instance detection so captured repetition collapses into reusable templates: vendor edit-distance (Apache-2.0, pure JS, no dependencies, dormant since 2022 but implementing the frozen 1989 Zhang-Shasha tree-edit-distance algorithm, and it takes your own children accessor and cost functions so it runs directly on our node types), then apply scrapinghub/mdr's verified heuristic — pick the candidate container nearest the element with the most text nodes, then tree-match its sibling subtrees — reimplemented in TypeScript since that repo is archived Python. A captured product grid then yields ONE template definition plus N instances, with .pairs() naming exactly which fields differ between instances and therefore which fields become template slots. This is the highest-leverage single step toward the owner's TEMPLATES requirement and the difference between exporting a design system and exporting six duplicated cards.
